cards.title: Smoke test angle validation with static image ads
cards.summary: Use one product-on-white image with different text call-outs to cheaply identify which value prop or angle earns clicks before investing in video.
cards.use_when: New product launch or angle selection: you have a modest test budget and need to find which value proposition makes people click before spending on video production.
steps: Take the same product-on-white image and keep it identical across variants.
Create a white bar with bold text (a call-out) over the image, changing only the message: e.g. 'reduce anxiety', 'increase focus', 'stress release'.
Run all variants in one simple campaign and read which call-out earns the most clicks/engagement.
When one call-out clearly wins, expand that single angle into video rather than making video for all angles.

For the video, decide whether the person on screen should be a man or a woman; consider not showing a face and instead showing only hands, arms or body type so more viewers can see themselves using the product.
After the ad-level test, move scrutiny to the landing page; keep testing ad performance in-platform to compare image vs video and value prop vs value prop.
Repeat the loop: image test, then video, then add creators, colours and regions to get more granular as winners emerge.
caveats: The source presents this as his own starting method, not a validated universal rule.
CPC/CPM baselines differ by niche (he cites $15-$30 CPM as niche-dependent); judge clicks against your own account history, not the source's numbers.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Diagnose price before scaling spend
cards.summary: Read cheap front-end click and cart metrics first; if traffic is cost-effective and carts still abandon, the price or offer is the problem, not the ad.
cards.use_when: Early-stage acquisition: deciding whether to spend more budget or change pricing after a first test tranche.
steps: Check whether clicks and impressions are cost-effective against your own niche baseline (the source notes CPMs vary widely by audience; hitting middle-America moms is expensive).
If people click the ad, click through to the PDP, reach the cart and then abandon, treat it as a price/value-exchange signal and change the price.
If people buy with good unit economics, the price point is working; if they get far along and don't buy, split-test the price.
Treat price and product playfulness as the first thing to figure out with a small learning budget, before blaming creative.
caveats: The source frames this as his own sequencing; his $15-$30 CPM range is illustrative and niche-specific, not a benchmark.

At larger spend and stronger email/retention assets, a cheap cost-per-cart may be worth keeping even when the final sale doesn't happen — a judgment the source reserves for brands that can monetise the backend.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Tranches of cash: define what each test budget must uncover
cards.summary: Frame your ad spend as learning tranches — a $10k tranche and a $500 tranche both buy the same lessons, just at different speeds.
cards.use_when: Budget planning for a launch or a channel test: deciding how much to allocate and what questions the money must answer before it's gone.
steps: Before spending, write the question the tranche must answer: is my price right, which channel is most efficient, which product works, what messaging?
Accept that a small budget learns the same things as a large budget but takes longer; velocity is the only difference.
In the first quarter, set the total tranche you can afford and treat it as a bet you must make work (the source's own launch example was $75k-$100k).
Run the front-end metrics in parallel with price: are people clicking the ad, clicking through the PDP, reaching the end, buying?
If unit economics are good, keep going; if not, isolate whether the break is creative, traffic cost or price.
caveats: The source's Breeze figures ($75k-$100k first quarter, doubling month over month) are his brand's example, not a promise.
He notes brands that can't survive without first-purchase profitability face a harder road, particularly if the product isn't repeat-purchasable.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: CAC targets anchored to LTV, not a universal number
cards.summary: Set target CAC from known customer lifespan and repeat behaviour, and accept a loss on first acquisition only when the backend justifies it.
cards.use_when: Acquisition planning: deciding your target and ceiling CAC, and whether to run first-purchase-profitable or loss-leading campaigns.
steps: Estimate how long customers stay and how often they rebuy for your specific product class; the source's working CAC is $85-$90 with a ceiling around $120-$130 on bad months.
State that target internally so media buying can be judged against it rather than daily ROAS.
If your product has repeat purchase or product expansion, you can justify spending to break even or a small loss on the first order.
If your product is a one-off (his examples: rugs, a t-shirt), plan to be first-order profitable because you won't recover the loss.
During launch on a brand-new product, budget extra for market education — teaching the category that the product is legitimate and legal can be part of the CAC.
caveats: His $85-$90 target and $120-$130 ceiling are his brand's figures and depend on his LTV; do not copy them as benchmarks.
Loss-leading on first purchase requires confidence in retention and backend conversion; without that it is simply unprofitable spending.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Organise the ad account by story, not by funnel stage
cards.summary: Replace strict top/middle/bottom funnel segmentation with asset-and-angle folders that carry one consistent story from ad to landing page.
cards.use_when: Account structure decisions for paid social: how to name, group and route campaigns and how much to rely on audience segmentation.
steps: Accept that the old three-tier funnel — prospecting for new customers, a value-prop middle, a discount-retargeting bottom — is now muddier and less segmented in practice.

Stop forcing audience segmentation to control which ad a new customer sees; that control was needed when the platform couldn't be trusted to serve the right creative, and the source argues we are now in a 'trust the algorithm' era.
Instead, build folders around your stories and angles: e.g. a 'feel better tomorrow' group that contains every video, image and landing page version of that story.
Keep the story consistent from the landing page all the way through the ad assets inside each folder.
Invest the saved effort into telling more convincing stories and building more offers, since landing pages can now be built or adapted in a day with current tools (verify current tools' interfaces).
caveats: This is the source's read of platform direction and his own account practice, not a platform mandate; some accounts may still benefit from tighter segmentation.
His claim that creative now outweighs audience selection rests on a platform engineering article he references, not on a controlled test.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Creative as the new targeting
cards.summary: Build ads whose cast, setting and language mirror the region and identity of the audience you're buying, because narrative now does the targeting work.
cards.use_when: Creative direction and casting for paid social: choosing who appears in ads and which regional variants to produce.
steps: Identify the market you're buying and match the people in the ad to it: the source reports ads with people who look like they've lived in Florida perform better in Florida, and New York-styled creative performs better in New York.
Treat a creative as stackable bricks — hook, value prop, benefits, problem, solution — and rearrange them for each audience or product claim.
Test granularity: for example, three women stating three effects within the first few seconds versus founders on camera; the source reports far longer retention when the viewer sees themselves.
In the briefing, specify the placement, framing and length, plus examples of what is working and examples of what has failed, so creators know the boundaries without losing their own voice.
Archive and reuse: keep an organised drive of past winning assets because long libraries are now a competitive asset for remixing into new clips.
caveats: Regional-matching results are the source's own-reported observations, not published benchmarks.
Continuously refreshing the library matters because asset styles age quickly.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Design creative natively for each placement
cards.summary: Build and brief separate assets for 4x5 and 9x16 placements instead of letting a square ad with cut-off captions run everywhere.
cards.use_when: Ad production and briefing: fixing poor performance caused by mismatched aspect ratios and unreadable captions on Reels and Stories.
steps: Decide the placements in advance (the source focuses on Meta) and produce assets at the correct ratios — he names 4x5 and 9x16 — rather than one square that gets reused everywhere.
Check that captions and the focal point of the creative are visible instantly in the chosen ratio; square ads with words and dots in a story are a common, fixable mistake.
In the creator brief, state the placement and format explicitly (e.g. 'this is for Meta Reels, we need 9x16 or 4x5'), plus framing rules such as shooting in sunlight.
Build the fix into the workflow: return creator footage that is too close or has the product cut off on the right for reshooting rather than shipping it.
Sort every concept into an image version and a video version for each placement — the source calls this more work but necessary at serious spend.
caveats: The exact ratios and platform behaviours can change; verify current placement specs in the ad platform before briefing.
The source says small brands may not be able to obsess at this level initially; it prioritises placement hygiene at higher spend.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Make the media buyer a P&L-aware creative strategist
cards.summary: Collapse the pod into a media buyer who also owns creative strategy and sees the P&L, with designers and editors supporting them.
cards.use_when: Team design for paid acquisition: deciding the roles needed to run ads and what performance reporting the buyer should own.
steps: Restructure from separate pods (creative strategist, account manager, media buyer, junior buyer, designer) to one owner who is both media buyer and creative strategist, supported by a designer and creators.
Put that person in direct contact with whoever owns creative strategy on Slack so iterations, hooks and asset formats move in real time.
Give them visibility of the P&L and forecasting so their decisions account for the whole business, not just an ad-platform ROAS widget.
Expect a media buyer who believes they control performance mainly through account settings to be replaced by one who manages creative supply.
Consider using an outside expert for a short weekly check-in while someone internal learns the account — the source used this as a hedge and short-term training.
caveats: The source's example is an internal hire who had never run an ad and was given four weeks to self-teach, supported by an existing creative team — not a guarantee for every brand.
He also says a freelance media buyer at a high level now needs designers and editors around them; the lone button-pusher is the role at risk.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Run a weekly creative volume target tied to spend
cards.summary: Measure new assets launched and winners that attract spend, then staff against the volume the season and profitability require.
cards.use_when: Creative operations and resourcing: setting a weekly production target and deciding when to hire editors or creators.
steps: Set a weekly target in concepts, not just assets — the source's example is 10 concepts with 2 ads each, 20 total, as a successful week.
Track two numbers per week: how many new assets launched, and how many hit the success metric, which he defines as dollars spent on them.
Adjust the target for season: product drops, Q3/Q4 and summer versus Q1 change the required volume and the profitability target.
Use the target to size the team: if the target doubles in busy season, that tells you when to hire against it.
Do not produce assets for SKUs that can't be sold — if products are backordered, funnel that time and money elsewhere.
Keep roughly a 30-day runway of assets, planning monthly and rotating in drops, holidays and evergreen angles.
When introducing new ads, avoid flooding the account: adding 5-15 new ads while only two or three proven ads carry spend can skew the whole account, which often forces the team to kill the new ads.
caveats: The 10 concepts/20 ads figure is the source's own weekly benchmark for one brand; it shifts with season and product drops.
Too much volume can destabilise a profitable account — the source explicitly names the tension between 'more assets' and 'we're unprofitable, kill everything'.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Think about the funnel in numbers: 70/30 to 90/10
cards.summary: Split spend between proven winners and tests, moving from 70/30 toward 90/10 or 100/0 when company performance is weak.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget inside a paid social account: how much to keep on convictions and how much to reserve for new tests.
steps: Target roughly 70% of dollars on assets you have conviction in and 30% on things you are unsure about.
When overall company performance is bad, shift to 90/10 — the source says even 100/0 is defensible then.

Time tests against where your sales actually come from: the source notes his product gets more energy Friday-Sunday, so spending heavily Monday-Thursday risks wasting budget that would perform better on the weekend.

Let the ratio flex daily based on profitability and on the platform's allocation behaviour — if Meta shifts spend to a non-converting ad, turning it off can stop the account from spending, so the buyer has to push and pull budgets rather than letting the account run limp.
Make sure you keep testing while new people are coming in, or the account eventually runs out of fresh winners.
caveats: 70/30 and 90/10 are the source's heuristics, not calculated from a dataset or universal rule.
The right ratio depends on how much proven creative you already have and how tolerant your unit economics are.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Judge ads on multiple KPIs, not dashboard profit alone
cards.summary: Combine CAC, email/text capture and CPM to decide which ads to keep, and blend results across channels rather than killing an ad on one platform's ROAS.
cards.use_when: Ad reporting and optimisation: deciding whether to switch off an ad or channel that looks unprofitable on its own dashboard.
steps: Use CAC as the primary success metric for a customer.
Treat email or text capture as a legitimate secondary KPI: if an ad gets people to cart cheaply, the source keeps spending because the address is captured and the backend can convert later.

Look at CPM as a softer third indicator, particularly on awareness-heavy placements that don't produce the highest-quality traffic but do reach people; the source says a small brand probably shouldn't let this drive decisions yet, while a larger one can.
Blend channels into one pot: an ad source (his example: Apple Search Ads) may lose on CAC but win on email collection, and the company-level question is whether total channels hit the goal CAC.

Coordinate spend with the rest of the business: if email flows, a product drop or a discount programme will land in the next days, pull back ad spend rather than overspending on customers who would buy anyway.
caveats: The 20% subscriber take rate he cites is his brand's figure; relying on email capture assumes your own backend can convert those addresses.
The 'let it run past profitability' approach is explicitly something he says works at his scale, not a rule for brands without strong retention and flows.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Match site experience to customer history
cards.summary: Show first-time, returning and high-value visitors different SKUs and messages based on what they have already bought.
cards.use_when: Site merchandising and CRM: deciding what a visitor sees on arrival based on purchase history.
steps: For a visitor who has never bought, communicate the SKUs they should try first, chosen from historical repeatability data.
For a returning buyer, do not show the same products they already bought; present a welcome-back message and what to try next based on what they have tried.
Segment by lifetime value: the source says someone who spends over $500 with them should be treated very differently from someone who has never seen the brand.
Build the depth of this journey deliberately — the message and product set should change with the customer's stage, not just the acquisition campaign.
caveats: Requires purchase history and some data depth; the source's $500 threshold is his own brand's example.
Works best with products that have continuation or expansion paths; a single-SKU store has limited levers.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Fix the homepage for your SKU count
cards.summary: Low-SKU stores should make the landing page almost a one-product conversion page; high-SKU stores should lead with offer, then bundles, then categories.
cards.use_when: Homepage and landing page design: structuring the first screens of a store based on how many products you sell.
steps: For low-SKU stores, keep the landing page close to a landing page with a little brand story; the single product should be added to cart or checkout as fast as possible with minimal extra clicks.
For high-SKU stores, put the current offer or promoted campaign in the header area where it gets the most visibility.

Directly beneath that, show the highest-AOV bundles and packs — the source points to True Classic's pack structure as an example — acknowledging that raising the first-order value is the goal for every store.
Further down, introduce categories so shoppers with many SKUs can browse, plus reviews and feedback for individual items.
Do not overcomplicate the number of pages at the start.
caveats: The True Classic reference is the source's example of testing volume, not a guarantee your store will match it.
High-AOV merchandising assumes your economics and fulfilment can support larger pack sizes.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Replace blank white PDP first images with lifestyle imagery
cards.summary: A product page whose hero is a plain product on white wastes prime real estate that could carry lifestyle context and a strong headline.
cards.use_when: PDP optimisation: revising the first image and adjacent copy on a product page.
steps: Audit the first image on each product page; if it is a plain product on white, replace it with a lifestyle image, the product in use, or a dynamic shot.
Put the strongest benefit headlines next to the hero rather than a weak description of why someone would buy.
Use the first-image choice as a split test to see whether lifestyle context lifts performance versus the plain shot.
Pair the visual change with the strongest angle discovered in your smoke tests so the PDP matches the ad that brought the visitor.
caveats: The source allows product-on-white can be a useful A/B variant, but calls it a wasted default, not an absolute requirement in every category.
Marketplace conventions (mentioned for Amazon) can differ from DTC norms; match the channel the shopper expects.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Use clipping marketplaces to scale distribution cheaply
cards.summary: Buy fixed-budget clip campaigns from low-cost creators who post to their own pages, paying only for approved posts and capped at your budget even if clips go viral.
cards.use_when: Acquisition creative sourcing: testing a paid clipper model to add volume and impressions beyond your own accounts.
steps: Choose an offer and state a budget plus a target CPM (the source's example: $5,000 at an 85-cent to $1 target CPM — a figure to treat as illustrative, not a benchmark).
Provide the creative brief and assets you want used so the clippers post material consistent with your angles.
Use the marketplace's approval step: you don't pay until you approve a post.
Accept the cap: if a clip goes viral and would be worth far more at the target CPM, you still pay only the agreed budget.
Expect the audience to be random pages driving to your site, which means you need an organised backlog of briefs and assets to keep feeding the army.
Treat follower counts as irrelevant; the source's framing is that impressions and traffic back to the store are what matter.
caveats: He predicted the tactic would become widely known and CPMs could rise as large advertisers enter; verify current marketplace terms and pricing before committing.
The clip model relies on clippers not needing the physical product, which may not fit every category or legal/compliance context.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Set up a testing pipeline and organic posting habit
cards.summary: Run a repeating image-to-video test tree across value props, male/female presenters and regions, and keep posting organically because it supports the ad account.
cards.use_when: Standing up a paid social testing process and deciding whether organic posting is worth the time for an ecommerce brand.
steps: Start the tree with image smoke tests, expand winners into video, then add creators, colours and regions as you learn.

Alongside the paid tests, post organically on your channels; the source reports that when the brand stops uploading assets to social channels, ad account performance weakens, and that organic content often becomes top-performing paid creative because it doesn't feel like an ad.
If you don't yet have an ad account, post on every platform as a starting practice — the source suggests twice a day as a best-practice target.
Route learnings back to creators quickly: share what is working in real time, including failed formats to avoid.
Use the pipeline to answer micro questions — which value prop, which presenter type, which region — and let answers feed the next round of briefs.
caveats: The claim that organic activity improves the ad account is the source's reported observation, not a documented mechanism; the twice-a-day cadence is his suggested practice.
Ad platform behaviour and current posting tools change — verify current platform guidance before building the calendar.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Build an always-on creative bench and 30-day asset runway
cards.summary: Keep testing and producing even when you have winners, because the account is the lifeline of new customers and stopping is not an option.
cards.use_when: Creative and media planning over a month or quarter: keeping a rotating pipeline rather than scheduling one-off production bursts.
steps: Assume more creative is better than less: with nothing working you need more anyway, and once something works it tells you what more to make.
Plan in monthly cycles, rotating in drops, holidays and evergreen angles that historically perform, and keep launching those plus new tests.
Keep testing while new customers are coming in, so the account doesn't run out of fresh winners.
Maintain roughly a 30-day runway of assets: you can build many variants off what is working now, but only about a month's worth before trends shift and the assets become obsolete.
Watch for the account being lopsided: if only a couple of proven ads carry spend and every new ad misses, the account can destabilise and the team may have to pull back the new launches.
caveats: The 30-day runway is the source's rule of thumb, not a calculated optimum.
He also acknowledges days when nothing is taking budget and the right move is to pull back rather than force spend.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Brief editors and designers with references plus brand context
cards.summary: Untrained editors replicate a reference pixel-by-pixel; the editor you want understands the reference, your brand and how to improve on it.
cards.use_when: Creative production and outsourcing: writing briefs for external creative help who understand performance marketing.
steps: Recognise that performance-aware editors are scarce and that using a generic designer to add badges or sparkle produces incoherent ads.
Give references explicitly and state this is an example of the outcome you want, then supply what your brand stands for and the assets and value props involved.
Tell the editor they should adapt the reference to your brand rather than copy it word-for-word or pixel-by-pixel.
Include examples of things that are working and things that failed, while telling creators to keep their own voice because they know their audience.
Expect that your own idea of what you want becomes clearer once you receive a first version, so budget for a second or third revision rather than judging the initial brief.
Source talent where time zones align (the source works with editors in Canada and Latin America for this reason) and verify current rates and platforms.
caveats: The source says brand owners often can't communicate what they want until they see something — plan for iteration rather than expecting a perfect first cut.
Talent-market and time-zone specifics change; verify current arrangements.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Learn the ad account yourself before hiring out
cards.summary: Founders and leadership should run ads up to roughly $10k-$30k of spend so they can ask better questions and avoid paying management on top of test budget.
cards.use_when: Early paid acquisition: deciding whether to manage ads internally or hand them to an agency or freelancer.
steps: Run the account yourself at the start, up to about $10k-$30k in monthly spend, so you understand what the eventual manager is doing and can ask better questions.
At very low spend ($3k-$10k/month), weigh the management fee against test budget: paying someone thousands more may leave too little to learn with, so eat the work yourself.
Use current tools; the source argues they are sophisticated enough that you don't need heavy outside support.
If you do want help, hire someone for a short consult or a weekly look over your shoulder rather than a full retainer.
Insert an outside expert for a limited weekly audit while an internal person learns — the source used this as a hedge during a handover.
caveats: The $10k-$30k threshold is the source's rule of thumb, not a computed break-even.
At higher spend the internal creative-strategist model with a P&L-aware owner becomes more viable than founder operation.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx

cards.title: Track daily burn, discount rate and high-value orders together
cards.summary: Understand your daily burn and your discount percent of sales so rising revenue doesn't hide shrinking margin.
cards.use_when: Finance and acquisition coordination: setting daily tracking and deciding when to pull ad spend or run promos.
steps: Track daily spend and return at the channel level each day — the source's team reviews spend and return hourly, Monday to Sunday.
Add discount as a percent of sales as a core metric and know your sweet spot; if sales rise while discount percent rises too, you may not be outrunning burn.
Track orders over $1,000 per day as an indicator of high-value customer activity.
Use discount dollars as a lever that trades off against ad spend: when media pulls back, promotions or discounts can fill the gap for those days.
Keep the marketing and finance forecast in the same conversation so spend changes are made with the daily cash position in mind.
caveats: Hourly, daily, always-on review reflects a brand at the source's scale; smaller brands may track less frequently but should still monitor burn and discount rate together.
The $1,000 order threshold is his brand's metric, not a universal target.
cards.source_name: The New Way to Run Meta Ads in 2025.docx
